learn.title: Adding to a pointer
learn.body: You can add whole numbers to a pointer. The key rule: `p + 1` moves by one item, not by one byte. For an `int *` it moves 4 bytes, for a `double *` it moves 8. The compiler multiplies by the item size for you.

learn.title: Moving and measuring
learn.body: This prints 3, 3, 12, then 2. `q - p` counts items between the pointers. The byte gap is 12, because 3 items of 4 bytes each lie between them. `p++` moves `p` to the second item.

learn.title: Walking an array
learn.body: `p` points at `a[0]` of `{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}`. Where does `p + 4` point?

learn.title: Staying in bounds
learn.body: Pointer arithmetic only makes sense inside one array, or one item past its end. Reading or writing outside it is undefined behavior: the program may crash, print garbage, or seem to work. The compiler does not check this for you.
`%td` prints the difference of two pointers, a `ptrdiff_t`. It counts items, not bytes.

questions.prompt: `p` is an `int *`. How many bytes does `p + 1` move?
questions.explanation: It moves one `int`, which is 4 bytes.

questions.prompt: `d` is a `double *`. How many bytes does `d + 1` move?
`q` is `a + 3` and `p` is `a`. What does `q - p` give?
questions.explanation: The subtraction counts items between them, not bytes.

questions.prompt: Reading outside an array is \_\_ behavior.
questions.explanation: The result is undefined: the program may crash or print garbage.

questions.prompt: After `p++` on an `int *`, what does `p` point at?
questions.explanation: `++` moves by one item of the pointed type.

questions.prompt: Match the expression to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic always counts in items.
